items.title: Core idea: how to read a risk register
items.body:
Many quizzes in this pack start from one row of the risk register. A risk register is a table a team keeps of things that could go wrong. Each row here has:

- **Risk**: a short name for the problem.
- **Evidence**: what in the code shows it.
- **File anchors**: the exact lines to open.
- **Impact** and **Likelihood**: how bad it would be, and how likely. Note phrases like "High if payments added": some risks only matter once the prototype grows.
- **Suggested test** and **Suggested fix**.
- **Confidence**: how sure the author is.

How to study a row: open the anchor, read the lines until you can say in your own words what the code does today, then decide whether the risk is a bug *now* or a trap for *later*. Do not trust the label alone; check it against the code.

excerpts.quote: | Risk | Evidence | File anchors | Impact | Likelihood | Suggested test | Suggested fix | Confidence |
| No tests | No test script |

readMore.why: The full table: ten rows, each with an anchor into the source.

items.title: The cost of products.find inside orders.map
items.body:
**Key: O(orders x products); build a Map keyed by product id once, then look up.**

For each order row, `products.find` scans the product list from the start until it finds a match. In the worst case that is every product, for every order: 50,000 x 5,000 steps. That nested-loop shape is O(orders x products). The standard fix, which the register suggests ("Map by ID or backend join"), is to build a `Map` from product id to product once (one pass over products), then each row is a constant-time lookup. The runtime guide stresses this is a scaling concern, not a bug at today's seed size.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Sort first so find becomes O(log n)*: `find` always scans in order; sorting does not change that.
- *Already linear*: the scans are nested, not one after the other.
- *React keys are the bottleneck; window the table*: the rows already have `key={order.id}`; the register points at the lookup.

excerpts.quote: const product = products.find((item) => item.id === order.productId)
| Order/product lookup scaling | `find` inside `orders.map` |
This is not a current performance bug; it is a scaling consideration.

items.title: What guards the Admin view: nothing but a state value
items.body:
**Key: only local UI state: setting the view key renders Admin, with no auth at all.**

The main area is a list of conditions, one per view: when `view === 'admin'` is true, the Admin component renders. `view` is ordinary React state. Whatever sets it to `'admin'` shows the Admin panels. The validation guide is direct: "No authentication, authorization, sessions, tenant scoping, API keys, role checks, or permission filters exist." Treat Admin as mock UI only.

Why the others are wrong:
- *ViewKey excludes 'admin' from the build*: the guide says `ViewKey` "prevents typoed local views, not unauthorized access"; types disappear when the code runs.
- *A signed session cookie, server-rendered*: there is no server and no session.
- *A role check for buyer sessions*: no roles exist anywhere in the app.

excerpts.quote: {view === 'admin' && <Admin />}
No authentication, authorization, sessions, tenant scoping, API keys, role checks, or permission filters exist.
- `ViewKey` prevents typoed local views, not unauthorized access.

items.title: Core idea: separate what the code does from what it claims
items.body:
The guides keep two lists apart: what the code does **today**, and what a **future** production version would need. Keep that split in your head for every quiz.

For "today", the only reliable source is the code itself. The screens use confident words about checkout, orders and admin tools; for each such screen, find the handler behind the button and list every effect it really has: which state it sets, what it writes to storage, whether anything leaves the browser. Text on a screen is not behaviour, so do not answer from the label.

The future-facing ideas the guides discuss (server-side prices, idempotency keys, role checks, outbox pattern, retries) are there so you can spot where a naive extension would go wrong. When a quiz asks "what happens today", answer from your list of real effects; when it asks "what is the risk if this becomes real", answer from the guide's production concerns.

excerpts.quote: ## Current Side Effects | Side effect | Evidence | Current reliability |

readMore.why: The production concepts: idempotency, retries, outbox, compensation, timeouts.

items.title: What "Order BG-98241 confirmed" really means
items.body:
**Key: nothing was issued: it is hardcoded JSX, and the order number is a literal.**

Pay now only flips `checkoutComplete` to true. The success box is plain JSX shown when that flag is true: the text "Order BG-98241 confirmed" and "Licenses, receipts, and delivery links were issued." are written directly in the source. Every buyer sees the same number. The trust row ("Fraud scoring, tax evidence, and license provisioning are enabled.") is also just text. The risk register files these under "Mock operational claims mistaken as real".

Why the others are wrong:
- *The order number is generated per purchase*: it is the literal string BG-98241.
- *An order record was saved to localStorage*: the only thing saved is the cart id list under `buildgum-cart`.
- *A receipt email was queued*: the side-effects guide says no email, queues or external APIs exist.

excerpts.quote: Order BG-98241 confirmed Licenses, receipts, and delivery links were issued.
| Mock operational claims mistaken as real | TLS/fraud/license text |
| UI checkout confirmation | [`src/App.tsx`](../../../src/App.tsx#L406-L414) | State-only; no external effect. |

items.title: Why filteredProducts is computed, not stored
items.body:
**Key: stale-copy drift: a stored filtered list could disagree with its sources.**

`filteredProducts` is recalculated from `products` and `query` on every render. If it were a separate piece of state, every code path that changes the query or the products would have to remember to update it too. Miss one, and the list on screen no longer matches its sources. The guide puts it as "duplicate state creates consistency bugs" and warns that "new query paths could forget it".

Why the others are wrong:
- *StrictMode effect corruption*: no effect computes this list; it is a plain expression in the component body.
- *Stale closures in handlers*: that is a different bug (an old value captured in a function); storing vs deriving the list is about two copies of the same facts.
- *Infinite render loops from a setter during render*: deriving calls no setter at all; nothing here sets state during render.

excerpts.quote: const filteredProducts = products.filter((product) => {
Why it matters: duplicate state creates consistency bugs.
- If filtering moved into a mutation handler, new query paths could forget it.

items.title: The headline risk of browser-side checkout math
items.body:
**Key: the client controls the amounts, so tampered totals get charged as-is.**

Subtotal, discount, tax and total are all computed in `Checkout` in the browser. Anything that runs in the user's browser can be changed by the user. If a payment call simply sent this total, a tampered value would be charged. That is why the register rates "Checkout math trusted if made real" High impact and suggests "Server-side price authority": the server must recompute prices itself.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Tax is wrong only for international buyers*: the rate is one hardcoded 0.0825; the runtime guide lists "Tax jurisdiction rules" as a production failure mode, and the main risk is still tampering.
- *Float drift of a cent is acceptable*: the guide calls JS numbers "risky for real money", and drift is a separate row (Money precision), not the headline.
- *Concurrent renders drop the discount*: nothing in the code or guides supports this.

excerpts.quote: const tax = (subtotal - discount) * 0.0825 const total = subtotal - discount + tax
| Checkout math trusted if made real | Client subtotal/discount/tax |
- Can client prices be tampered with? Future checkout must use server-side price authority.

items.title: Why " build20 " still matches BUILD20
items.body:
**Key: yes: the lookup trims and uppercases the input before comparing.**

The discount lookup is `discounts.find((discount) => discount.code === promo.trim().toUpperCase())`. `trim()` removes the spaces and `toUpperCase()` turns build20 into BUILD20, so the comparison matches. The validation guide lists exactly this: "Trim/uppercase before lookup", and notes the remaining risk: expiry and bounds are ignored.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Applies only on a second render*: the lookup is computed during render from the current `promo` value; there is no delay.
- *Fails HTML validation*: the promo input has no validation attributes; it is a plain controlled input.
- *Exact, case-sensitive comparison*: the input is normalized first, so case and padding do not matter.

excerpts.quote: const appliedDiscount = discounts.find((discount) => discount.code === promo.trim().toUpperCase())
| Promo code | Trim/uppercase before lookup. |

items.title: Where a wrong-shape cart value finally fails
items.body:
**Key: not at the parse: the cast lets the object through, and cartIds.map then throws.**

`{"id":1}` is valid JSON, so `JSON.parse` succeeds and returns an object. The `as string[]` after it is a TypeScript *type assertion*: it tells the compiler "trust me", and it is removed from the running code. Nothing checks the value, so the object becomes `cartIds`. The first place that treats it as an array is the derive `cartIds.map(...)`; a plain object has no `map` method, so that call throws. The validation guide's row: "Type assertion after parse ... No runtime shape validation."

Why the others are wrong:
- *TypeScript drops non-matching values at runtime*: TypeScript does nothing at runtime.
- *The persistence effect refuses non-arrays*: `JSON.stringify` serializes objects fine; the effect has no check.
- *JSON.parse rejects a non-array top level*: any JSON value, including an object, parses.

excerpts.quote: return stored ? (JSON.parse(stored) as string[]) : [products[0].id]
const cartProducts = cartIds .map((id) => products.find((product) => product.id === id))
| Cart storage | Type assertion after parse. |

items.title: Why a double click on Pay now does no harm today
items.body:
**Key: it only sets a local checkoutComplete flag, and no request exists to duplicate.**

The button calls `onComplete`, which the parent passes as `() => setCheckoutComplete(true)`. Setting a flag to true twice leaves it true; no order is created and nothing is sent. The guide's worry is about the future: once a real payment call is wired in here, repeated presses could create duplicate orders, so the system will need idempotency keys and server-side order state.

Why the others are wrong:
- *An idempotency key makes the second click a no-op*: no such key exists; the guide says a real system *needs* one.
- *The button disables itself after the first click*: it is disabled only when the cart is empty (`disabled={!cartProducts.length}`).
- *React batches both clicks into one*: two separate clicks are two events; the handler runs each time, it is just harmless.

excerpts.quote: onComplete={() => setCheckoutComplete(true)}
<button className="primary-action full" disabled={!cartProducts.length} onClick={onComplete} type="button">
a real system needs idempotency keys and server-side order state.

items.title: What "Add to cart" does for an item already in the cart
items.body:
**Key: the id list is unchanged, but the product is selected and checkout resets.**

`addToCart` calls three setters. The first one, `setCartIds`, checks `current.includes(product.id)`: if the id is already there it returns `current` unchanged, otherwise it appends. The other two always run: `setSelectedId(product.id)` and `setCheckoutComplete(false)`. So the cart stays the same, but the product becomes the selected one and any shown confirmation is cleared.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Quantity increments*: there is no quantity anywhere; the cart is a list of unique ids.
- *Returns early before its setters run*: there is no early return; the includes check lives *inside* the first setter's callback.
- *A second copy is appended*: the includes guard prevents duplicates.

excerpts.quote: setCartIds((current) => (current.includes(product.id) ? current : [...current, product.id])) setSelectedId(product.id) setCheckoutComplete(false)
- Add unique cart ID: [`src/App.tsx`](../../../src/App.tsx#L73-L74)

items.title: A saved id for a removed product: hidden, but still stored
items.body:
**Key: the item vanishes from the cart, but its id stays in storage.**

`cartProducts` maps each id to a product with `find`. For a removed product `find` returns `undefined`, and the next `.filter((product): product is Product => Boolean(product))` drops it. So the buyer simply does not see it. But the persistence effect writes `cartIds`, the raw id list, not `cartProducts`. The stale id stays in state and is written back to localStorage. Display and storage quietly disagree.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The initializer prunes unknown ids*: it only parses; it never checks ids against the catalog.
- *Rendering crashes on undefined*: the filter removes `undefined` before anything renders it.
- *A placeholder row is shown*: dropped entries are not rendered at all.

excerpts.quote: .map((id) => products.find((product) => product.id === id)) .filter((product): product is Product => Boolean(product))
window.localStorage.setItem('buildgum-cart', JSON.stringify(cartIds))

items.title: Start here: Buildgum as a one-file React prototype
items.body:
Buildgum is a small creator-commerce prototype: a storefront, a cart, a checkout screen and some admin dashboards, all in the browser. It is built with Vite, React and TypeScript, and almost everything lives in one large file, `src/App.tsx`. Seed data is in `src/data.ts` and the types are in `src/types.ts`.

This pack uses four pages of the `docs/upskill/` curriculum. Read them in this order:

1. **docs/upskill/00-fast-track.md**: run it, then trace the storefront and checkout flows.
2. **02-stack-and-language-mastery/01-language-runtime-model.md**: browser APIs, derived data, array operations, money.
3. **03-architecture-and-patterns/03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md**: what is validated today and what a senior would check.
4. **03-architecture-and-patterns/04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md**: today's side effects and what a real checkout would need.
5. **08-reference/risk-register.md**: one table of the main risks, each with file anchors.

Every guide links exact lines in `src/App.tsx`. Keep that file open and jump to each anchor as you read.

excerpts.quote: The app has one large UI module with local state, derived data, and view switching in [`src/App.tsx`](../../src/App.tsx#L49-L168).
By Sunday night you should be able to run Buildgum, explain the main UI state, trace storefront-to-checkout

readMore.why: The curriculum overview and the recommended path for each level.
Commands that were verified, and the first two flows to trace.

items.title: What corrupt cart JSON does at startup
items.body:
**Key: JSON.parse throws in the useState initializer, crashing the app before it renders.**

The cart state is created with an initializer function: it reads `buildgum-cart` and, if there is a value, calls `JSON.parse(stored)`. There is no try/catch. A truncated array is not valid JSON, so `JSON.parse` throws while React is creating the component's first state, and the app never renders. The register's fix is a "Safe parser" plus a malformed-localStorage test.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Falls back to the seeded default*: the fallback `[products[0].id]` is used only when nothing is stored; a stored but broken string goes to `JSON.parse`.
- *React catches it and renders an empty cart*: the app has no error boundary or catch here.
- *The type predicate filters it out*: that filter runs later on ids; the crash happens before any state exists.

excerpts.quote: const stored = window.localStorage.getItem('buildgum-cart') return stored ? (JSON.parse(stored) as string[]) : [products[0].id]
| Corrupt cart storage crashes app | `JSON.parse` without catch |
- `JSON.parse` throws if stored data is corrupt.

items.title: What an unmapped status does to the badge
items.body:
**Key: class 'pill archived' gets the neutral .pill rule and no status colour.**

The badge's class is built from data at runtime: `pill ${product.status.toLowerCase()}`. An Archived product gets `pill archived`. In `style.css`, the base `.pill` rule (beige background) still matches, but colour rules exist only for live, review, paused and draft. There is no `.pill.archived`, so the badge shows the neutral look. TypeScript cannot see this gap because CSS class names are plain strings, which is why the register asks for explicit maps and fallbacks.

Why the others are wrong:
- *React warns about an unknown className*: React does not know which classes CSS defines; any string is accepted silently.
- *The row fails to render*: there is no "pill map" in the code; the class is just a string.
- *Styled the same as Draft*: draft has its own `.pill.draft` rule with a red colour; the neutral `.pill` rule looks different.

excerpts.quote: {product.status}
.pill { background: #eee8db; color: #4b463f; }
.pill.draft, .risk.high { background: #ffe8e5; color: var(--red); }
| Status/risk style drift | Data-derived class names |
